summary: Specifies the OpenPGP message formats, which provide public key and symmetric encryption, digital signatures, compression, and key management. It exists so developers can build interoperable applications and is not a step-by-step cookbook. It obsoletes RFC 4880, RFC 5581, and RFC 6637.

eli5.summary: OpenPGP is a way to lock and sign messages so only the right person can read them. This document explains the format everyone must follow.

questions: what is the difference between v4 and v6 openpgp keys
subtitle: The message, key and signature formats behind PGP-style encryption, now with modern curves and authenticated encryption.

tldr.problem: People and programs need a common, interoperable way to encrypt data, sign it, and exchange the public keys and certificates that make both possible.
tldr.mechanism: OpenPGP defines a stream of typed packets: session keys encrypted to recipients or passphrases, an encrypted data container, signatures, and key packets bound together by signatures. Optional ASCII Armor turns the binary stream into printable text.
tldr.outcome: RFC 9580 is the current revision. It obsoletes RFC 4880, RFC 5581 and RFC 6637, adds version 6 keys and signatures, X25519 and Ed25519, AEAD encryption and Argon2, and deprecates weak legacy choices.

today: RFC 9580 is a Proposed Standard published in July 2024. It obsoletes RFC 4880, RFC 5581 and RFC 6637, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: What OpenPGP Provides
sections.content:
RFC 9580 specifies the message formats used in OpenPGP: encryption with public key or symmetric algorithms, digital signatures, compression and key management. It is a revision of RFC 4880, which revised RFC 2440, which replaced RFC 1991. It also obsoletes RFC 5581 (Camellia in OpenPGP) and RFC 6637 (elliptic curves in OpenPGP).

The document says what it is and is not. It is maintained so developers can build interoperable applications. It is not a step-by-step cookbook, and it does not deal with storage and implementation questions, though it does discuss implementation issues needed to avoid security flaws.

Confidentiality works in two layers. The sender generates a random session key for each message, encrypts the message with a key derived from it, and encrypts the session key to each recipient's public key. Each session key is used only once. Signing hashes the message and signs the digest with the sender's private key. Both services can be applied to the same message: sign first, then encrypt the message plus signature.

An implementation MAY support compression, and SHOULD support base64 conversion (ASCII Armor). Signature-only subsets that omit encryption are described as non-conformant only in that omission.
sections.eli5: Imagine sealing a letter in a box with a one-time key, then locking that key inside a smaller box only your friend can open. Signing is like adding a stamp that only you can make.

sections.title: Packets, Headers and Criticality
sections.content:
An OpenPGP message, keyring, certificate or detached signature is a sequence of packets. Each packet has a header, which carries a Type ID and the length, followed by a body. The length in the header is the canonical source of packet boundaries, and a parser MUST NOT read octets outside the range the header gives.

There are two header formats. The current OpenPGP format has bits 7 and 6 of the first octet set to one and the Type ID in bits 5 to 0, so it can encode IDs up to 63. The Legacy format has bit 6 zero and only 4 bits for the Type ID. Legacy packets MAY be read but SHOULD NOT be generated.

OpenPGP format lengths come in four forms: 1 octet (up to 191), 2 octets (192 to 8383), 5 octets (up to 4,294,967,295) and Partial Body Lengths, which are powers of two from 1 to 230 that turn a packet into a stream. Partial lengths may only be used for literal, compressed or encrypted data packets, and the first one MUST be at least 512 octets.

Type IDs 0 to 39 are critical: an unknown critical packet means the whole sequence MUST be rejected. IDs 40 to 63 are non-critical and an unknown one MUST be ignored. This gives a safe way to add new packet types later.
sections.eli5: Every piece of the message is wrapped in a labelled envelope that says what it is and how big it is. If you meet an envelope marked really important that you do not understand, you must stop.

sections.title: Keys, Subkeys and Certificates
sections.content:
An OpenPGP certificate (a Transferable Public Key) starts with a primary Public Key packet. The primary key MUST be able to make signatures, because it creates self-signatures. It is followed by User ID packets, each with certification signatures, and by optional subkeys, each with a Subkey Binding signature from the primary key. Subkeys may be encryption, signing or authentication keys, and the RFC calls it good practice to use a separate subkey for each operation. A subkey that can sign must carry an embedded Primary Key Binding signature (type 0x19).

Version 6 certificates store key flags, expiry and algorithm preferences in a self-signed Direct Key signature (0x1F), and an implementation MUST ensure a valid one is present before using a version 6 key. This blocks attacks that strip a self-signature that carries an expiration or preferences. User IDs are explicitly optional. A version 6 revocation certificate must include the primary key packet, so it is self-verifying.

Keys are identified by a fingerprint and an 8-octet Key ID. The Key ID is not assumed unique. Version 4 uses SHA-1 and version 6 uses SHA2-256, with the 0x99 or 0x9B prefix, a length, and the whole Public Key packet hashed. Version 3 keys are deprecated and MUST NOT be generated.
sections.eli5: Your main key is like a master ID card. Subkeys are spare keys for specific jobs, such as locking or signing, and the master card vouches for each one.

sections.title: Signatures and Their Types
sections.content:
A Signature packet binds a public key to some data. Version 4 and 6 signatures carry a hashed subpacket area, covered by the signature, and an unhashed area that has no cryptographic protection and is advisory only. An implementation MUST generate a version 6 signature with a version 6 key and a version 4 signature with a version 4 key, and MUST NOT create version 3 signatures.

The signature type says what the signature means: signing a document, certifying that a key belongs to a User ID, binding a subkey, revoking a key, and so on. The RFC calls the vagueness of the certification types a feature, because the receiver has final authority over validity. In practice most implementations issue generic certifications (0x10).

Version 6 signatures add a random salt that is hashed first. This makes signatures non-deterministic, removes any attacker-controlled hash prefix, and guards against repeated signatures over the same message. The salt size depends on the hash algorithm and is at least 16 octets. For messages, a One-Pass Signature packet lets the signer hash in one pass and put the Signature packet after the data.
sections.eli5: A signature is like a wax seal pressed with your own ring. The seal also says what it means: I wrote this, I vouch for this person, or this key is no longer valid.

sections.title: Encrypted Messages and the Two SEIPD Versions
sections.content:
An encrypted message is zero or more session key packets followed by an encryption container. A PKESK packet carries the session key encrypted to a recipient's public key; an SKESK packet carries it encrypted under a key derived from a passphrase. A message can mix both, so it can be opened with a passphrase or a private key. A recipient may be hidden: a version 3 PKESK can use an all-zero Key ID and a version 6 PKESK can omit the fingerprint, so the receiver tries every private key.

The container is the SEIPD packet. Version 1 uses CFB mode and appends a Modification Detection Code: two constant octets 0xD3 0x14 and a 20-octet SHA-1 hash. Version 2 uses an AEAD mode in chunks. It has a cipher ID, an AEAD ID, a chunk size octet and 32 octets of salt. The message key and IV are derived with HKDF using SHA256. The chunk size is 1 << (c + 6), and an implementation MUST NOT create a chunk size octet above 16 (4 MiB chunks). A final tag over the empty string includes the total plaintext length, so truncation is detected.

Packet versions must match. Version 3 PKESK and version 4 SKESK go with version 1 SEIPD; version 6 PKESK and SKESK go with version 2 SEIPD. A version 2 SEIPD MUST NOT be preceded by the older packets.
sections.eli5: The message sits in a strongly sealed box. Next to it are little notes, each holding the box's key locked for one friend, or locked behind a password. The new box also notices if someone cuts off the end.

sections.title: ASCII Armor and Cleartext Signatures
sections.content:
Because some channels only carry printable text, OpenPGP defines ASCII Armor: base64 wrapped in lines of no more than 76 characters, between a header line and a tail line. Header lines are surrounded by five dashes, for example BEGIN PGP MESSAGE, BEGIN PGP PUBLIC KEY BLOCK, BEGIN PGP PRIVATE KEY BLOCK and BEGIN PGP SIGNATURE. Armor Headers are not protected by any signature.

The old optional 24-bit CRC footer is now discouraged. A receiver MUST NOT reject data because the footer is present, missing or wrong, and the footer MUST NOT be generated for messages ending in a version 2 SEIPD packet or for version 6 keys and signatures. The Version header SHOULD NOT be emitted, to minimize metadata.

The Cleartext Signature Framework signs readable text, with a BEGIN PGP SIGNED MESSAGE header, dash-escaped text and an armored signature. Trailing spaces and tabs are removed before signing, so it cannot safely round-trip text where whitespace matters, such as a unified diff. For such data the RFC says to use a signed message or a detached signature instead.
sections.eli5: Armor is a way to write secret code using only ordinary letters and numbers, so it survives being pasted into an email without getting scrambled.

sections.title: Algorithms and Passphrase Protection
sections.content:
The algorithm tables use numeric IDs. Implementations MUST implement Ed25519 (27) for signatures and X25519 (25) for encryption, and SHOULD implement Ed448 (28) and X448 (26). They MUST implement AES-128 and SHA2-256, and the AEAD mode OCB. RSA keys are deprecated and SHOULD NOT be generated; Elgamal and DSA keys MUST NOT be generated. IDEA, TripleDES and CAST5 MUST NOT be used to encrypt, and MD5, SHA-1 and RIPEMD-160 MUST NOT be used to generate signatures.

Passphrases are turned into keys with a string-to-key (S2K) specifier. Simple S2K MUST NOT be generated. Argon2 (specifier type 4) is RECOMMENDED because it is memory hard. It stores a 16-octet salt, the number of passes t, the parallelism p and an encoded memory size, where memory is 2encoded_m KiB. Iterated and Salted S2K MAY be used when Argon2 is unavailable.

Secret keys protected by a passphrase record how in the S2K usage octet: 253 means AEAD, 254 means CFB with a SHA-1 check, and 255 (MalleableCFB) is for reading old keys only. Argon2 is only used with AEAD protection.
sections.eli5: The rules list which locks are strong enough to use today, and which old ones you may only open and never build. A good passphrase is also stretched so that guessing it takes a very long time.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC's central warning is ciphertext malleability. If an attacker can change ciphertext and still get plaintext out, attacks such as the quick check oracle become possible. If an AEAD tag fails, the implementation MUST NOT parse or release the decrypted data and MUST halt. Senders SHOULD use version 2 SEIPD when all recipients support it, and implementers should implement AEAD promptly. The deprecated SED packet MUST NOT be generated.

Other points include: SHA-1 is not collision resistant but is still needed for version 4 fingerprints; PKCS#1 padding errors should be handled in constant time or reported as a single error; comparing long fingerprints by eye is unreliable; and a compression quine could exhaust resources, so implementations SHOULD limit layers of decompression.

Metadata is also covered. A Padding packet can hide message or certificate length, an Intended Recipient Fingerprint subpacket helps stop surreptitious forwarding, and subpackets in the unhashed area should not be trusted for important decisions. Reusing a session key to reply (the v2 SEIPD feature) can silently expose a reply to the wrong readers, so the RFC says to prefer fresh public key encryption when possible.
sections.eli5: The safety rules say: if the box looks tampered with, throw it away without peeking, and do not trust notes that are written on the outside of the envelope.

sections.title: What Changed From RFC 4880
sections.content:
Appendix B gives implementers upgrading from RFC 4880 and RFC 6637 a summary. New or added items include Ed25519, Ed448, X25519 and X448, the version 2 SEIPD packet with OCB (mandatory), EAX and GCM, version 6 keys, signatures, PKESK and SKESK packets, AEAD secret key protection, Argon2, SHA3-256 and SHA3-512, the Padding packet, packet criticality, and the Intended Recipient Fingerprint subpacket.

Deprecated items include RSA weak keys, DSA, Elgamal, MD5, SHA-1 and RIPEMD-160, IDEA, TripleDES and CAST5, Simple S2K, MalleableCFB, the Symmetrically Encrypted Data packet, version 3 keys and signatures, the Revocation Key subpacket and the CRC footer in ASCII Armor.

Some terms were renamed: Radix-64 is now ASCII Armor, the old and new packet formats are the Legacy and OpenPGP formats, and Packet Tag became Packet Type ID. Appendix C lists errata incorporated into the text.
sections.eli5: This new edition adds stronger locks and bans the old rusty ones, and it gives some old words new names.

items.label: Text Signature
items.desc: Signature of text with line endings converted to CR LF.

items.label: Standalone Signature
items.desc: Signs only its own subpacket contents.

items.label: Generic Certification
items.desc: Binds a User ID to a key, with no claim about checking.

items.label: Persona Certification
items.desc: No verification of the identity claim was done.

items.label: Subkey Binding
items.desc: Primary key states that it owns the subkey.

items.label: Primary Key Binding
items.desc: Signing subkey states that the primary key owns it.

items.label: Direct Key
items.desc: Signature calculated directly on a key.

items.label: Key Revocation
items.desc: Revokes the key it is calculated on.

items.label: Certification Revocation
items.desc: Revokes an earlier certification or Direct Key signature.

items.label: Third-Party Confirmation
items.desc: A signature over another Signature packet.
